In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. McCoy Smith, Chair of OSI’s License Committee, presented “Open Source Licensing 101.”

Open Source Licensing 101

This essential session is a basic primer on what the Open Source Initiative is, the Open Source licenses they approve, and the broader categories those license fall into. Also included are tips for understanding the OSI license approval process and the Open Source Definition and Open Source AI Definition. An overview of some of the more prominent approved Open Source licenses was provided. Other related topics like best practices, available resources and other information for working best within Open Source was also provided.

OSI Licensing 101

Start with the fundamentals of Open Source licensing and intellectual property.

Video transcript

So, my name is McCoy Smith. I’m a lawyer in private practice in Oregon. But I’m also a member of the OSI board and I’m here to talk about legal stuff on open source.

By the way, for those of you who are working in-house at a corporation, you’ve probably heard a lot of this stuff already from your mandatory legal training. So, I apologize if that’s duplicative. Although, I do have some stuff that’s specific to the OSI in here that might be new to you if you’re not familiar with it.

So let’s talk about fundamentals first. What is open source? We’re at an open source conference. I assume most of you know what open source is. I would hope so.

But in essence, the Open Source Definition, which is promulgated by the OSI, defines how one thinks about what makes a piece of software open source. In a nutshell, an open source license allows you to do kind of whatever you want with the software without restriction.

There are a bunch of other criteria that they have there as well to understand how open source software works. This is the Open Source Definition, which was put together by the Open Source Initiative, I don’t know, over 25 years ago and has been fairly static since then. There have been debates around the margins about what some of these things mean, but in order for a license to be approved to be open source and to be listed on the list of licenses approved by the Open Source Initiative, it’s got to meet all these criteria. A couple of these are highlighted in green. They are among the most important and the ones people often fall afoul of when they’re attempting to work around the margins of open source or come up with new licensing models.

Specifically, over the past 25 years, various people have made an effort for various reasons to come up with licenses that discriminate in some way either against persons or groups or fields of endeavor. They submit them to the OSI, and very often the objection has been that they violate criterion five or six and can’t be approved. But all of these things are looked at when licenses come in for approval by the OSI.

So what is a license? A license is essentially a legal agreement. In the context of open source software, it’s a legal agreement that grants the receiver of whatever technology is being provided to them permissions to do a variety of different things with that technology oftentimes in exchange for certain obligations they must fulfill if they exercise those permissions.

So a software license is nothing more than the person who owns rights in that software giving somebody else permissions to do certain things with it. And very often they will say, “In return for the permissions I am giving you to use this software, I will expect you to fulfill the following obligations with regard to that software.” And then there are any number of variations on the obligations that may be imposed on the user.

Now, open source software licenses, like almost all software licenses, derive their legal effect primarily from copyright. So copyright is an intellectual property right that exists worldwide through various international treaties as well as national federal legislation in the United States and other countries. If you write something that’s considered a work of authorship, you have copyright rights in it and you have the right to control what people do with those rights and can dictate to them via license or some other legal mechanism what they’re allowed to do and not do with it.

With software licenses, you typically specify whether people have the right to use it, modify it, make copies of it, and distribute it.

Now, I’m not going to go into a lot of detail on this. Copyright protects expression, not functionality. So, there is a longstanding debate amongst lawyers and courts about what the distinction between those two things is. In fact, we will probably see at some point in the 150 or whatever litigations that are currently pending on the various AI systems greater explication of this difference because it’s going to be important when determining whether what the AI companies are currently doing by training on various copyrighted materials makes use of the expressive content in those materials, and if so, whether that’s permitted under copyright law. It’s an incredibly complicated question and courts and lawyers have wrestled with it for, I don’t know, a hundred years, and they’re still wrestling with it and we will maybe get some more clarity on this sometime in the future as a result of all these AI cases that are pending.

Another form of intellectual property protection is a patent, which is a little bit of the reverse of copyright. So it protects the functionality not the expression in any particular form of technology. It’s a little bit more complex to secure that sort of protection. You actually have to go to the government and say, “Here is what my technology does. Please review it and grant me patent rights to that technology.” It’s a relatively complicated process. I’m a patent lawyer, so I’ve done it for many years. But in the end, you also can get protection for the functionality through patent.

When you take a look at a software license, including an open source software license, you will often see it express permissions under both copyright and patent rights. Now, not all of them do that very clearly, and that’s another item that we lawyers love to debate about. But if you look at a fairly well-written software license, including an open source software license, it will typically say, “Under my copyrights, I give you the rights to do X, Y, and Z. Under my patents, I give you the right to do A, B, and C, and in return for those licenses that I grant to you, here are the three or four things that I expect you to do when exercising.” That’s basically how you put together a license for software.

Now, there’s a thing called copyleft, which is a clever turn of phrase on the concept of copyright. It was first coined by the Free Software Foundation and refers to the idea of using a license to self-perpetuate itself to ensure that the software that is attached to that license continues to be licensed under the same terms and conditions.

The reason this sort of licensing model was developed was so that somebody could release something open source and everybody who received it would be under the same obligation to release any variation they made of it as open source, whether they forked it or modified it. The idea was, “You have to live by the same rules that you got the software under. You can’t change the rules for yourself.” So it’s essentially a self-perpetuating legal instrument that ensures that a piece of software always stays under the same terms and conditions and remains open source forever.

Here are some examples of copyleft licenses, or reciprocal licenses. The most famous one is the GPL. Version 2 is used for the Linux kernel. Various other components of a Linux system are under GPLv2, GPLv3, AGPL, or LGPL.

The Free Software Foundation promulgates all these versions of the GPL. There are a lot of nuances between them, but they’re all intended to be self-perpetuating copyleft licenses and to ensure that the software and its source code stay under the same terms. LGPL is a variation that’s often called a weak copyleft and it says you have to abide by the self-perpetuating open source requirements of the license, but there are a couple exceptions. If you do the following things with the software, we’re not going to require those uses to replicate the license and provide the source.

The Mozilla Public License is the one you have for the Mozilla browsers and other things that Mozilla does. It’s like LGPL in that it’s a weak copyleft license. It requires code to be open source unless you use it in certain ways.

So that’s the first broad category of open source licenses. There’s another type of open source license, the non-copyleft licenses. The most famous of these are BSD and MIT. You probably encountered these because they’re pervasively used in open source all over the place. The Apache license is another example, from the Apache Software Foundation. It’s very commonly used and if you were in the presentation before this, Duane pointed out that the Apache license is becoming commonly used in AI.

These things are oftentimes called permissive licenses although some people object to the use of that terminology. So non-copyleft is kind of the more preferred but the main difference here is it’s not a self-perpetuating license. You are allowed to create your own fork and potentially attach a different license than the one that you got it under. Some people find that model preferable to the copyleft license because it gives more flexibility to the downstream user if they want to do something with it in a way that they don’t want to attach the same license to it. These licenses allow that.

Okay. So that’s open source law 101 in a nutshell in 10 or 15 minutes. All right, let’s talk about the current state of open source licensing.

So the OSI maintains a list of approved licenses. Those are licenses that somebody has submitted to the OSI, saying, “Please review this license, certify that it meets the Open Source Definition, and add it to the approved list that you maintain on your website.” If you’re looking for an open source license, there’s over a hundred of them on there, so you can probably find one that’s going to do what you want.

We do get about 25 to 30 submissions of new licenses every year. People come up with some kind of new license and say, “Hey, I’d like you to review this, compare it against the Open Source Definition, and let me know whether you can add it to the list.” Most of them get rejected primarily because of two faults. One is they don’t meet the definition. So they come in saying, “Please approve this,” when the license already fails to meet the definition at the time of submission.

The other is you get a lot of unclear drafting. So, there’s a bunch of lawyers on this approval list, including me, and we scrutinize these things to make sure they’re not written in an ambiguous way or are destined to be overturned by a court later or something like that. This problem is exacerbated a little bit recently by the people who think, well, they can get an AI to write it for them rather than a lawyer. That oftentimes doesn’t work either. So don’t think that the use of AI at the moment is a substitute for using a lawyer to write a license.

Anyway, we had 26 licenses submitted over the past year. Four were approved. I think all four of them were legacy licenses, which means these are licenses that have already been in use for a number of years. They have a lot of uptake by projects.
